meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 13: the exit map, where consultants go, when they leave and what each firm opens up
meldungen.text:
For most people who join a strategy firm, the job is a launchpad rather than a destination. Only a small minority ever make partner; everyone else leaves at some point, and the question that matters is not whether but when and where. After twelve instalments on individual firms and practices, this one draws the overall map: the main exits, the moments at which they open, and what each type of firm does to your options.

The first window opens after roughly two years, typically just before or after promotion from analyst to associate or consultant. Coaching sources and recruiters describe this as the classic exit point. The prize most people chase here is private equity: headhunters run tightly scheduled "on cycle" processes for pre-MBA associates, and they draw disproportionately from Bain, McKinsey and BCG, with Bain's PE group especially prominent because commercial due diligence is close to what a fund does. Corporate strategy and in-house consulting teams also recruit heavily at this stage, as do growth-stage start-ups looking for a "chief of staff" or business operations lead. Leaving much earlier, say after less than a year, mainly buys you the brand on your CV rather than the full skill set, and the options are correspondingly narrower.

The second window comes after project leader or engagement manager, usually four to six years in. By then you have run teams and clients, which changes what you are hired for. The typical moves are a director or head of strategy role in a large company, a senior operating role in a portfolio company of a PE fund, or a move into venture capital, where operational credibility counts for more than spreadsheet speed. A LinkedIn-based study of McKinsey, Bain and BCG alumni reported by Poets and Quants found that about one in eight became directors after leaving, and roughly a third continued as consultants or individual specialists elsewhere: a reminder that many exits are sideways rather than upwards.

The third window, after principal or associate partner, is narrower but higher. Here the exits are C-level or divisional leadership, partner roles at smaller firms or funds, and founding with enough network and capital to raise money quickly. Family offices also hire at this level, often for a single trusted generalist.

Firm type shapes the map. MBB keeps every door open, and especially private equity. Roland Berger and the Big Four strategy arms are strongest for industrial companies, the German Mittelstand and transaction work. Restructuring specialists lead to distressed investing and CFO tracks; boutiques such as Simon-Kucher or zeb tie you to their niche, which is valuable if you want to stay in it. Tech-heavy units like QuantumBlack or BCG X open product and start-up roles.

For your set of schools, the master matters mostly for the first door. A MiM from HEC, HSG or LBS is a recognised entry ticket to MBB in Paris, Zurich, Munich or London, and therefore to the two-year PE window. WHU and INSEAD carry particular weight in DACH and in the MBA-level relaunch some consultants use after three or four years.

meldungen.titel: German consumer watchdog sends formal warnings to Anthropic and OpenAI over pricing clauses and subscription changes
meldungen.text:
The Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen, a state consumer protection body in Lower Saxony, has issued formal warnings (Abmahnungen) to Anthropic and OpenAI. Under German law, such a warning is the first step before a lawsuit: the company is asked to sign a binding undertaking to stop the contested practice, and if it refuses, the watchdog can go to court. Both letters went to the firms' Irish subsidiaries, which serve European customers.

The complaint against Anthropic centres on two points. First, its terms reserve the right to change prices and plans at its own discretion. German rules on subsequent contract changes are strict: the grounds for any change must be named in advance and must be legitimate, and a blanket clause does not meet that test. Second, Claude subscriptions are advertised with prices that exclude tax. That is normal in the United States, where sales tax varies by state and is added at the till, but in Germany the full price including VAT must be shown.

OpenAI is accused of opaque changes to its Plus subscription. The company plans to merge the chat and work areas, pool the usage allowances for ChatGPT and Codex, and switch metering from the number of messages to tokens. The watchdog argues that customers cannot tell what this means for their actual allowance, and that they may end up buying paid extra credits more often for the same use. Digital products, it says, may only be changed for a valid reason, the effects must be explained clearly, and no extra costs may arise. Both firms are also criticised for a hard-to-find imprint that names no legal representative.

OpenAI is already being sued by another consumer body, in Brandenburg, over cumbersome cancellation of ChatGPT subscriptions and a one-sided price clause; it refused to sign an undertaking after a warning in July. Neither company had commented by the time of publication. The next step is whether Anthropic and OpenAI sign the undertakings or let the cases go to court.

meldungen.titel: Cervical cancer is falling sharply among young women in Germany, the first generation vaccinated against HPV
meldungen.text:
Germany's largest health insurer, the AOK, said on Friday that a long-term analysis shows a clear drop in cervical cancer among young women since HPV vaccination was introduced. The study followed women born between 1992 and 1994, the first cohorts who could get the vaccine as a statutory insurance benefit when it arrived in 2007, at the age of 13 to 15. Up to the age of 31, they recorded about 25 new cases per 100,000 women, a markedly lower rate than in earlier generations.

The finding fits a pattern that has been building for several years. Data from the insurer Barmer show that among women in their twenties, new diagnoses fell to roughly a third of their 2011 level by 2022, while women in their thirties, who were too old for the childhood programme, saw no such decline. That contrast is what makes the vaccine effect hard to dismiss: the same screening system, the same period, but a fall only in the vaccinated age groups. An earlier analysis by the AOK's research institute WIdO found that women vaccinated young needed surgery to remove precancerous tissue only a little over half as often as unvaccinated women.

The sobering part is uptake. The AOK has repeatedly complained that vaccination rates among teenagers have stalled, and German coverage remains well below countries such as England, where researchers estimate the programme has already prevented around 200 cervical cancer deaths.

For adults, the picture is more complicated. Protection is strongest when the vaccine is given before any exposure to the virus, which is why programmes target children. Catch-up vaccination later still helps against strains a person has not yet met, but it is usually not free once the age limits of public programmes are passed.

meldungen.titel: The Supreme Court will decide whether Trump can suspend asylum at the border without Congress
meldungen.text:
The US Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the asylum ban that President Trump proclaimed within hours of returning to office in January 2025. The question is constitutional as much as practical: can a president, by proclamation, override federal immigration law passed by Congress and unilaterally suspend access to asylum at the southern border? Two lower federal courts have rejected the administration's argument, but the ban has largely stayed in force while the litigation continues.

The ban is one part of a broader overhaul. The administration has also cancelled thousands of pending asylum applications and reshaped the immigration courts through mass dismissals of judges. In December the Supreme Court will separately review the practice of deporting asylum seekers to third countries that have agreed to process their claims, and a third case concerns the indefinite detention of people in deportation proceedings.

The administration's case rests on outcomes. In court filings it calls the measure a necessary defence against an "invasion" and against abuse of the system by people who are really seeking work. Border crossings have indeed collapsed: Customs and Border Protection recorded fewer than 100,000 apprehensions at the southwest border in the 2026 fiscal year, about 95 percent fewer than the annual average under President Biden. Simon Hankinson of the conservative Heritage Foundation argues that most arrivals would not qualify for asylum anyway and could have claimed protection in Mexico.

Critics, led by the American Civil Liberties Union, argue that the combined measures have hollowed out a legal right Congress created, stripping applicants of due process and turning the immigration courts into an arm of enforcement. They point to approval rates: according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University, more than nine in ten asylum claims were denied in June, compared with roughly half in 2024. Lawyers cite cases such as an Ethiopian torture survivor whose claim, they say, would previously have been straightforward.

With its conservative majority, the court has often given the executive wide latitude on immigration, but the case goes to the heart of the separation of powers. A ruling against the administration would not reopen the border overnight; it would restore the right to apply.

meldungen.titel: Germany: the Bundestag passes a tiered sugar tax on soft drinks from 2028, but the revenue goes to the budget, not to health
meldungen.text:
The decision. On Friday the Bundestag passed the Haushaltsbegleitgesetz, a package accompanying the federal budget, which introduces a tax on sugary drinks from 2028. It applies to drinks with at least 5 grams of sugar per 100 millilitres, such as lemonades, iced teas, energy drinks and sweetened fruit drinks, in three tiers: 25 cents per litre for 5 to 7 grams, 30 cents for 7 to 9 grams and 35 cents above that. Drinks sweetened with artificial sweeteners, juices without added sugar, alcohol-free beer and alcoholic drinks are exempt, as are small independent producers. The same law cuts the electricity tax for one year and raises the tax on spirits by a fifth.

The case made. Supporters, including the Finanzkommission Gesundheit that originally recommended the levy, argue that a tax nudges manufacturers to cut sugar and consumers to buy less, reducing obesity, diabetes and tooth decay and, in the long run, health spending. Critics from the drinks industry and parts of the farm lobby call it a revenue grab dressed up as health policy, and point out that manufacturers may simply swap sugar for sweeteners. The trade publication topagrar summed up that view as "a cash box instead of a health prescription".

The numbers. The best real-world test is Britain's Soft Drinks Industry Levy, introduced in 2018 with a similar tiered design. According to the UK government, the sugar content of drinks in scope fell by almost half between 2015 and 2024, mostly through reformulation before the levy even took effect. The main academic evaluation found a modest health effect, including a fall in obesity of about 1.6 percentage points among girls in their final year of primary school, and fewer hospital tooth extractions in children. On revenue, the Finance Ministry's draft projected about 900 million euros in 2028, according to Börsen-Zeitung, flowing entirely into the federal budget rather than into health insurance as the commission had proposed.

Reality check. The claim that a tiered levy cuts sugar in drinks is well supported by the British data. The claim that it measurably reduces obesity is supported only weakly: the clearest effect appears in one subgroup, and long-term results are still being monitored. The health argument also sits uneasily with the revenue projection, which stays high for years and therefore assumes that manufacturers will not reformulate as fully as they did in Britain. Whether the money should fund health care or the general budget is a value judgement that data cannot settle. The effect of replacing sugar with sweeteners remains genuinely uncertain.

Evidence rating: Partly grounded. The reformulation effect is backed by solid evidence from Britain, but the health benefits are modest and uncertain, and the budget logic partly contradicts the health rationale.
